items.followUp: Explain how stomata contribute to transpiration pull.

rubric.why: Identifies the loss of water vapour from leaf tissues as the starting point.
rubric.description: Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and exits through stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing evaporation from the leaves or mesophyll.

rubric.why: Explains how water loss creates the force that draws water up the plant.
rubric.description: Evaporation creates tension (negative pressure) in the xylem, pulling water upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the tension in xylem to the upward pull of water.

modelAnswer: Water evaporates from the moist mesophyll cells of leaves and diffuses out through the stomata.
This water loss creates tension (negative pressure) in the xylem, pulling the continuous column of water upward from the roots.

items.followUp: Distinguish between absorption and assimilation in nutrition.

rubric.why: States that ingestion is the intake of food.
rubric.description: Ingestion is taking food into the body through the mouth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of ingestion.

rubric.why: States that digestion breaks food down into simpler substances.
rubric.description: Digestion is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of complex food into simple, soluble substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of digestion.

modelAnswer: Ingestion is the taking of food into the body through the mouth.
Digestion is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of complex food into simple, soluble substances that can be absorbed.

items.followUp: Name three foods that are rich sources of carbohydrates.

rubric.why: Identifies plants as the main source of carbohydrates.
rubric.description: Plants make carbohydrates by photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying plants or photosynthesis as the source.

rubric.why: Gives examples of foods that supply carbohydrates.
rubric.description: Examples include cereals and foods such as rice, wheat, maize, potatoes, sugarcane and fruits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving suitable examples of carbohydrate sources.

modelAnswer: Plants make carbohydrates by photosynthesis.
Common dietary sources include cereals such as rice, wheat and maize, as well as potatoes, sugarcane and fruits.

items.followUp: What is manure? Give two examples of organic fertilizers.

rubric.why: Defines fertilizers by their use in supplying nutrients or improving soil fertility.
rubric.description: Fertilizers are substances added to soil to supply nutrients and improve its fertility for plant growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition or purpose.

rubric.why: Names the two main types of fertilizers.
rubric.description: The types are organic fertilizers and inorganic (chemical) fertilizers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both types.

modelAnswer: Fertilizers are substances added to soil to supply nutrients and improve its fertility for plant growth.
The two main types are organic fertilizers and inorganic (chemical) fertilizers.

items.followUp: Describe how minerals dissolved in soil water reach the leaves of a plant.

rubric.why: Describes the entry of water into the plant.
rubric.description: Root hairs absorb water from the soil, mainly by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming root hairs and water absorption (osmosis where specified).

rubric.why: Shows the route water takes through the root to reach the conducting tissue.
rubric.description: Water passes through the root cortex and enters the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing passage through the root to the xylem.

rubric.why: Identifies the tissue that carries water upward through the plant.
rubric.description: Water and dissolved minerals move upward through xylem vessels in the stem to the leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying xylem as the transport tissue.

rubric.why: Explains the forces responsible for the upward movement of water.
rubric.description: Transpiration pull is the main force; cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help maintain the water column. Root pressure may also assist.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for explaining transpiration pull and at least one supporting force or mechanism.

modelAnswer: Root hairs absorb water from the soil, mainly by osmosis.
Water passes across the root cortex and enters the xylem.
Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved mineral salts upward through the stem to the leaves.
Transpiration from leaves creates a pull that draws the water column upward.
Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help keep the column continuous; root pressure may also assist.

items.followUp: State the rules for writing the scientific name of an organism, using humans as an example.

rubric.why: Defines the two-part structure of a binomial name.
rubric.description: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word scientific name: genus followed by species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the name has two parts and identifying them.

rubric.why: Checks the capitalization rule for the genus name.
rubric.description: The genus name begins with a capital letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct capitalization of the genus.

rubric.why: Checks the capitalization rule for the species name.
rubric.description: The species name begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct capitalization of the species.

rubric.why: Checks the formatting rule for scientific names.
rubric.description: The two words are italicized in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either accepted formatting convention.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter.
Both words are italicized when printed; when handwritten, each word is underlined separately.
For example, the scientific name of humans is *Homo sapiens*.

items.followUp: Compare aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration, giving the products of each.

rubric.why: Answers that food can be broken down without oxygen and names the process.
rubric.description: Yes. Food can be broken down in the absence of oxygen by anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear yes and identification of anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Identifies the conditions or nature of the process.
rubric.description: Anaerobic respiration is an incomplete breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the absence of oxygen or incomplete breakdown.

rubric.why: Names a common organism or method associated with anaerobic breakdown.
rubric.description: In yeast, this process is called fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast or fermentation.

rubric.why: Gives the products of anaerobic breakdown in yeast or muscle cells.
rubric.description: Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscle cells can produce lactic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct product set.

rubric.why: Notes that anaerobic respiration releases energy.
rubric.description: The process releases a small amount of energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is released.

modelAnswer: Yes. Food can be broken down in the absence of oxygen by anaerobic respiration, an incomplete breakdown of glucose.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration is called fermentation and produces ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy.
In muscle cells, glucose may be broken down without oxygen to form lactic acid and release a small amount of energy.

items.followUp: Name the conducting tissues in plants and state the function of each.

accept: more than one type of cell
rubric.why: Defines compound tissues as groups made of different cell types working together.
rubric.description: A compound tissue consists of different types of cells working together to perform a function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition.

rubric.why: Identifies xylem and its transport function.
rubric.description: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the rest of the plant; it includes vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming xylem and its function.

rubric.why: Identifies phloem and its transport function.
rubric.description: Phloem transports prepared food from leaves to other parts of the plant; it includes sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem and its function.

rubric.why: Provides structural details or recognizes both conducting compound tissues.
rubric.description: Xylem and phloem are the two compound tissues; suitable component cells include vessels and tracheids in xylem, and sieve tubes and companion cells in phloem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both tissues or giving suitable component cells.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues are made of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to other parts of the plant; it consists of vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma.
Phloem transports prepared food from leaves to other parts of the plant; it consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma.
